Purchased because of the utter over-hype of the VRO mod from @BeardoBenjo.

Well, that mod was jank at launch.  So we waited.  And waited.  And waited.
And its still jank.   Yet he still cranks out a video on RoN every month ranting about how great it is.

Anyway, our group gave up and played it flat just to extract some value from the game.

This is repetetive. And not in a fun way.

Suit up in heavy, get a shotgun. Shoot the door open (why even bother using the 'tactics' it just slows you down.  Shoot the bad guy (assuming it actually lets you hit them) and rince and repeat.

Failed a mission?  Never mind! Carry on anyway!  It doesn't matter, they're all the same.

The base game isn't even fun, so him ranting over the VRO mod like the second coming of the lord is ridiculous.  The next week he hyped up Aces of Thunder, another game that tanked when real people got to play it.

I guess you can't trust online reviewers, thank god for the user reviews here.

If you like repetetive boredom with dumb-ass AI and enemies who are either invincible or just stand around while you shoot someone right next to them, buy this.

Weird thing is, I like this game. Played it a lot. Have not left a review before because I thought they might sort out the problems with one of the DLCs or something, but I have been waiting for them to fix the AI of your dudes in single player forever now. 

Several DLCs released and you still have to mod the game to fix the AI and that only works a little. They will not respond to commands sometimes, will not face angles properly etc. Some rooms they are fine but others they will just not know what to do. They will flashbang themselves and you. You can have four fellas stacked up on a door, guns ready, someone opens the door before you breach and two of your men will be dead before they decide to shoot the guy. Sometimes they will just get confused by a door being open inwards or something and take about 6 seconds to get into the room after a flashbang. Very frustrating that you feel like you cant let them do anything reliably. Also I wish the gas was a bit more powerful but its probably realistic haha.

Everything else in the game is cool, guns are really good, shooting feels great. Love shooting peoples hands off with shotguns. The sound is fantastic, music it good. Only performance problems I had were in the last level for where I got some weird lag spikes, other frame drops were not that bad and my pc is pretty old with a 2060. 

But very cool game, just cant recommend the single player. If you intend to play this with friends though that wont be a problem of course. So negative but good game lol. Hopefully they fix it one day but I doubt it at this point.

It's overall a reasonably good game with most of its systems being well-fleshed out. However, the balancing needs some work, and the enemy AI needs to have their crack taken away. It's been almost 3 years now, people have been constantly telling VOID that the AI are skynet terminators, and they have stubbornly refused to acknowledge this and fix them. So I'll stubbornly refuse to give this otherwise good game a positive review, because it is ruined by atrocious AI, which become way worse on Hard difficulty and require bug abuse or incredible luck to finish missions.

Other problems include the SWAT AI being complete nincompoops by comparison, excessive suppression effects on the player yet enemies suffer no such thing as suppression, ridiculous and unrealistic weapon sway while moving, no rubber bullets for the dozens of guns we have, some traps being virtually invisible and impossible to manually disarm (either due to being hard to see or because some particular doors don't swing out far enough), bomb vest suspects can still get animation locked (stun one by any means, then start disarming the bomb before they recover), and there really isn't a good reason why we should have to take terrorists alive; and any armed suspect in general conscious; for the best score. Many of the missions also don't have great variety and some missions are more linear than they really need to be, especially Relapse. If you're going to make it so that players have to restart a mission over and over again to clear it, why not at least allow for more variety and routes?

Finally, the DLC are overpriced and the base game doesn't really have enough content to justify buying at full price. No, the taser does not need to be nerfed again. It was fine after the first time, stop nerfing it.

I've been following Ready or Not since the pre-orders first launched, so I've been around since the early days of the game. It's been great seeing how much the game has developed over time, especially with all the new content that has been added.

I haven't had a chance to jump back in and experience all of the newer content yet, but the time I have spent playing has been enjoyable. Whether I was working toward achievements or simply playing through missions, I always had a good time.

Ready or Not offers a different kind of experience compared to most shooters, and I really enjoy the tactical approach it takes. There's plenty to do, and even just going through the missions and trying to complete everything makes for a good experience.

I still need to come back and check out everything that's been added, but based on the time I've spent with it, I'd definitely recommend Ready or Not.

Ready or Not is the spiritual successor to the classic SWAT games, and it does an excellent job of capturing what made them so enjoyable.

If you're looking for a fun, action-packed CQB experience, I genuinely don't think there's a better game on the market right now. There's something incredibly satisfying about watching your AI squad breach doors, clear rooms, and methodically work their way through hostile environments.

Whether you're approaching situations tactically or diving straight into the action, Ready or Not delivers an immersive and satisfying experience.

I highly recommend Ready or Not, especially to anyone who grew up playing the classic SWAT games or enjoys tactical shooters.

I Came for a Tactical Shooter. I Left a Different Person.

There are games you play to pass the time. There are games you play because you're bored. There are games you play because your friends are online.

And then there is Ready or Not.

I genuinely don't know how to put into words what this game has done to me. I installed it expecting a tactical shooter. I expected guns, missions, suspects, some good old-fashioned door kicking and perhaps the occasional questionable decision from my teammates.

I was not prepared.

I was not prepared for the silence before entering a room. I was not prepared for the sound of footsteps on the other side of a door. I was not prepared for the moment when a suspect refuses to surrender, when a teammate shouts for cover, or when everything goes horribly wrong in a fraction of a second.

But most importantly, I was not prepared for the emotional journey.

Every mission feels like it means something. Every corner feels like it could be your last. Every time I hear someone shout "POLICE, DROP YOUR WEAPON!" I feel a little part of my soul leave my body.

And yet, I keep coming back.

I have laughed. I have screamed. I have questioned my intelligence. I have stared at a loading screen wondering where my life went wrong. I have watched my carefully coordinated tactical operation collapse because one person forgot to check a corner.

But I have also experienced moments of genuine brilliance.

The feeling of clearing a building with your squad, covering each other, communicating properly and somehow making it through an entire mission without everything descending into absolute chaos is something I struggle to find in any other game.

There is something special about a game that makes you slow down. A game that makes you think before you act. A game that reminds you that sometimes the most important thing you can do is NOT pull the trigger.

And that is what makes Ready or Not so special.

It isn't simply about shooting people. It is about restraint, responsibility, teamwork and the weight of the decisions you make.

The atmosphere deserves its own appreciation. The sound design, the lighting, the environments, the voice acting, the tiny details scattered throughout every mission. Everything contributes to an experience that can be genuinely uncomfortable in the best possible way.

There are moments where I have genuinely forgotten that I am sitting at a computer playing a video game. I am no longer thinking about my keyboard or mouse. I am thinking about the room ahead, the people inside it and whether my squad is going to make it out.

And then someone on my team gets stuck in a doorway.

Immersion shattered. Humanity restored.

I also want to acknowledge the people behind this game.

To the developers, artists, sound designers, programmers, writers, animators and everyone else who contributed to this project: thank you.

I know that making a game is not easy. I know that behind every little detail that players might overlook are hours of work, problem-solving, frustration and dedication.

Most players will probably never stop to appreciate the amount of effort that goes into making a single mission feel believable. They might never think about the sound of a distant gunshot, the positioning of an object in a room or the way an environment tells a story without saying a single word.

But somebody made those decisions.

Somebody cared enough to make those details exist.

And somebody, somewhere, spent an unreasonable amount of time making sure that a door opens in a particular way.

I hope those people know that their work matters.

Because it does.

Games like this remind me why I love gaming in the first place. Not because of graphics, not because of achievements, not because of how many hours I can put into something, but because of the experiences that games can create.

The memories.

The ridiculous moments with friends.

The missions that go perfectly until the final thirty seconds.

The missions that go catastrophically wrong from the very first door.

The times when everyone is silent because something genuinely terrifying just happened.

And the occasional teammate who thinks a flashbang is a substitute for basic communication.

I don't know how many more hours I will spend playing Ready or Not. I don't know how many more missions I will complete, how many more times I will get shot through a doorway, or how many more times I will have to explain to my squad that perhaps we should try a slightly different approach.

But I do know one thing.

Years from now, when I look back at the games I played, I suspect Ready or Not will be one of the ones I remember.

Not because it was perfect.

Not because every update was flawless.

Not because every mission went according to plan.

But because it made me feel something.

And that is becoming increasingly rare.

So, to everyone at VOID Interactive: thank you for creating something that people can genuinely lose themselves in. Thank you for putting so much detail into a game that could so easily have been just another shooter. Thank you for giving us something worth talking about, laughing about, getting frustrated with and returning to.

And to whoever designed the AI that can somehow identify my exact location through three walls, a filing cabinet and what I can only assume is divine intervention:

I hope you sleep well.

You have ruined my life.

In the best possible way.

I gave this game a negative review because apparently players are expected to fix it themselves!

If, like me, you're experiencing severe LOD (Level of Detail) and texture pop-in issues, here's a potential fix:

Press  Win + R and enter:

`%LOCALAPPDATA%\ReadyOrNot\Saved\Config\Windows`

Open Engine.ini and add the following lines:

[SystemSettings]
r.ViewDistanceScale=5
r.StaticMeshLODDistanceScale=0.1
r.SkeletalMeshLODBias=-2
foliage.LODDistanceScale=3

Save the file and restart the game.

These settings increase rendering distances and force higher-detail models to remain visible at greater distances, reducing noticeable LOD transitions and object pop-in.

Be aware that this may reduce performance depending on your hardware, although I personally haven't noticed any measurable difference.

It's ridiculous that players have to resort to manually editing configuration files to fix such obvious graphical issues. This is something the developers should have addressed themselves, not left to the community to figure out.
